words: The process a plant uses to make its own food from sunlight, water, and air.
Light energy from the Sun. Plants capture it with their leaves to power food-making.
The ability to do work or cause change. Sunlight gives plants the energy they need to grow.
The plant part that captures sunlight and takes in air. Leaves are where photosynthesis happens.
The food plants make during photosynthesis. Plants use sugar to grow, flower, and make seeds.
The underground plant parts that absorb water and minerals from the soil and send them up the stem.

parts.title: Plants Make Their Own Food
parts.html:
Animals eat food to get energy. Plants do something different: they make their own food. The process is called photosynthesis.

A plant captures sunlight and uses it to turn water and air into sugar. That sugar is the plant's food. It gives the plant energy to grow new roots, stems, leaves, flowers, and seeds.

parts.title: Leaves, Roots, and Air Work Together
parts.html:
Three things go into photosynthesis: sunlight, water, and air. Leaves face the sun and soak up light. Tiny openings in leaves let air in. The plant uses one gas from the air, called carbon dioxide.

Roots pull water up from the soil. The water travels up the stem to the leaves. Inside each leaf, the plant combines sunlight, water, and air to make sugar. The sugar travels through the stem to every part that needs energy.

parts.title: How We Know Sunlight Matters
parts.html:
Scientists figured this out by taking sunlight away. A plant kept in the dark stops making food. Its leaves turn yellow, and it gets smaller and weaker.

A plant in bright light stays green and keeps making sugar. Same plant, same water: the only difference is light. That difference is the evidence that sunlight is the key ingredient.

compare.testDo: Drag the paper-towel strip under one tray and the dark paper under the other, or tap each one, then tap a tray. Press Turn on sun and water. Then swap them and press it again.
compare.disclaimer: This is a model. Paper isn't alive, but the idea is the same: a towel soaks up water from below, and dark paper soaks up sunlight from above.

Atowel.text: The paper-towel strip, like these roots, soaked up the blue water. The water climbed right up it!

Adark.text: The dark paper just got soggy in the wet soil. There's no sunlight underground to soak up. Try the towel strip here.

Bdark.text: The dark paper, like these leaves, soaked up the sunlight and got warm.

Btowel.text: The towel strip sat in the sun, but there's no water up here to soak up. Leaves get their water from the roots. Try the dark paper here.

compare.frame: This ___ is ___, so its job is to ___.

curator.A: Grows in wet soil → takes in water. Roots spread through the soil and soak up water, like the towel strip. The water travels up the stem to the leaves.
curator.B: Spreads out in the sun → catches sunlight. Leaves are wide and face the light, like the dark paper. Tiny openings let air in, too. Inside the leaf, sunlight, water, and air become sugar.

wall.locked: Brush the level above first. The elevator goes down, one level at a time.
wall.first: Brush the glowing top layer. Drag across it (or tap it again and again).
wall.next: Going down the tree. Brush Level {n}.

wall.rule: Every part of a plant has a job. Roots take in water, the trunk or stem carries it up, and the leaves use sunlight, water, and air to make sugar.

mix.q: The leaves made the sugar. Does all of the sugar stay in the leaves?

options.t: Yes. The leaves keep all the food they make.
options.miss: Not quite. Sugar travels down the branches and trunk to the roots, the fruit, and the seeds. Every part needs energy.

options.t: No. Sugar travels to the branches, trunk, roots, fruit, and seeds.
options.ok: Yes! The leaves make the food, then share it with every part of the tree. That's how sugar ends up in an orange.

wow.title: A tree that breathes with you
wow.alt: A huge, wide live oak tree with long, low branches
wow.caption: Fairchild Oak, one of the biggest live oaks in Florida. Bulow Creek State Park, today.
wow.html:
Every leaf on a tree is covered with tiny openings. Air goes in, and the tree keeps one gas from it: carbon dioxide.

Scientists estimate a grown tree takes in about 48 pounds of carbon dioxide each year. As it makes sugar, it lets out oxygen, the gas you breathe!
wow.insetCap: One tiny opening on a tomato leaf, seen with a very strong microscope. Scientists added the green color.

keyIdea: Plants make their own food through photosynthesis. They use sunlight, water, and air to make sugar, which gives them energy to grow. Leaves capture light. Roots absorb water.

quiz.q: What three things does a plant combine to make food during photosynthesis?

options.miss: Think about the diagram: something comes in from the sun, something travels up from the roots, and something comes in through the leaves. What are those three things?

options.ok: 🌿 Yes! Sunlight, water, and air are the three ingredients. Plants use them to make sugar, their food.

options.miss: Think about the diagram: something comes in from the sun, something travels up from the roots, and something comes in through the leaves. What are those three things?

quiz.q: What would most likely happen to a plant kept in total darkness for many weeks?

options.t: It would grow faster because it is resting.
options.miss: Remember: sunlight is the energy source for photosynthesis. Without it, the plant has no way to make food. What do you think would happen then?

options.t: It would keep making food from the water in the soil.
options.miss: Remember: sunlight is the energy source for photosynthesis. Without it, the plant has no way to make food. What do you think would happen then?

options.t: It would stop making food and its leaves would turn yellow.
options.ok: 🌲 Exactly right. Without sunlight, photosynthesis stops. The plant can't make food, so it weakens and its leaves lose their green color.
